analysis.one_liner: Made it much harder for investors to sue companies over securities fraud.
analysis.headline: The Senate passed it 69-30 on June 28, 1995, and Congress made the same provisions law that December over President Clinton's veto.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill raised the bar for shareholders suing over securities fraud: complaints had to allege specific facts showing the company acted with intent, evidence-gathering froze while a judge decided whether to throw the case out, damages were capped, and most defendants became liable only for their own share of fault. It also cut the deadline for suing to two years after the fraud is discovered and took securities fraud out of a federal anti-racketeering law that allowed triple damages. Alongside those protections for companies, it required outside auditors to look for corporate fraud and added rules reining in class-action lawyers.
analysis.who_benefits: Publicly traded companies, their executives and directors, underwriters, and outside accountants gain protection from costly shareholder fraud lawsuits, including class actions. Small companies that were frequent targets of lawsuit-driven "strike suits" also gain relief.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Publicly traded companies, executives, and auditors

how_it_helps.text: Requires plaintiffs to plead specific facts creating a 'strong inference' that the defendant acted with intent, and freezes discovery while a motion to dismiss is pending, filtering out speculative or meritless suits that small companies said were used to force quick settlements.
Replaces mostly joint-and-several liability with proportionate liability, so a peripheral defendant (like an outside director or an advisor) no longer pays for the full fraud committed by others.
Creates a safe harbor shielding executives from liability over forward-looking statements about projected performance, letting management speak freely about forecasts.

Requires independent auditors to design procedures to detect illegal acts with a direct and material effect on the financial statements, identify material related-party transactions, and evaluate going-concern doubt — and to report unremedied illegal acts to the company's board and, in some cases, to the SEC.

Restrains class-action practices that benefited lawyers more than investors: bans broker referral fees from attorneys, ties attorneys' fees to amounts actually recovered, requires disclosure of settlement terms, and caps named plaintiffs' recoveries at the same rate as other class members.

analysis.who_pays: Investors who lose money to corporate fraud — including ordinary people whose retirement savings are in stocks — bear the cost. With a much higher pleading standard, frozen discovery, a two-year filing deadline, capped damages, and liability limited to each defendant's share of fault, fewer claims survive to trial and recoveries are smaller when fraud is proven.

drawbacks.text: Defrauded investors face far higher barriers: they must plead specific facts giving a 'strong inference' of intent before they can gather any evidence, and discovery is stayed while the court weighs dismissal — so many valid claims, where the proof of intent lies inside the company's records, are thrown out at the start.
The filing deadline is cut to the earlier of two years after the fraud is discovered or five years after it occurred, wiping out longer-established state-law deadlines investors previously relied on.

Proportionate liability shifts uncollectible shares onto investors: if a responsible party is insolvent or settles cheaply, the people harmed absorb the loss, with only a narrow exception for small individual plaintiffs (net worth under $200,000).

The safe harbor for forward-looking statements protects rosy projections even when they turn out misleading, and the amendment to the RICO statute strips securities fraud victims of treble damages under that law.

Good-faith supporters acknowledged the strike-suit problem was real, but critics warned the cure would shield genuine fraud as well — the same pleading and liability rules apply whether the claim is frivolous or the fraud is egregious.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For companies, executives, underwriters, and their insurers the relief was large and immediate: fewer meritless suits, lower settlement exposure, and no more being the 'deep pocket' who pays for everyone else's fraud. The bill also delivered real safeguards — auditors must now actively hunt for corporate fraud, and class-action lawyers' fees are tied to what shareholders actually recover. But the price is paid by investors: the same tools that filter out bad suits also kill good ones, deadlines are shorter, and recoveries are smaller. On balance, the measure traded some genuine litigation abuse for a substantially weaker private-enforcement system, with the savings flowing to corporate defendants rather than to shareholders.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate passed the bill's provisions as an amendment to a House bill by 69-30 on June 28, 1995, and that package was enacted into law in December 1995 over President Clinton's veto.

narrative.text: Sen. Pete Domenici introduced the bill on January 18, 1995 with 51 cosponsors — 38 Republicans and 13 Democrats.
The Senate Banking subcommittee on securities held four days of hearings in March and April 1995, and the full committee reported the bill with a substitute amendment on June 19.
On June 22, Sen. Arlen Specter moved to send the bill to the Judiciary Committee, a stalling step; the Senate tabled the motion 69-19 (Republicans 46-3, Democrats 23-16).

After five days of floor debate, the Senate agreed to the committee substitute, folded the measure into H.R. 1058 as an amendment, and passed H.R. 1058 in lieu of S. 240 by 69-30 on June 28, 1995 — Republicans 49-4, Democrats 20-26.
The Senate action made the House bill the vehicle, and the resulting Private Securities Litigation Reform Act became law that December after Congress overrode President Clinton's veto.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Corporate issuers, executives, underwriters, and their insurers came out ahead: the liability protections became permanent law. Defrauded investors and the class-action plaintiffs' bar came out behind, with weaker recourse against real fraud.

sides.party_line_note: The bill passed with strong bipartisan support — 69-30, with 49 of 54 Republicans and 20 of 46 Democrats in favor — and had 13 Democratic cosponsors, but opposition was concentrated among Democrats, who supplied 26 of the 30 no votes.

industries.industry: Publicly traded corporations and their executives
industries.note: The bill shields issuers and management from shareholder fraud suits through higher pleading standards, frozen discovery, a safe harbor for optimistic projections, capped damages, and a shorter filing deadline. Their gain comes directly out of investors' ability to recover when fraud costs them money.

Auditors take on new mandatory fraud-detection, related-party, and going-concern procedures with civil penalties for ignoring them — but they also gain proportionate liability protection and, in the reported bill, a self-disciplinary board largely run by the accounting profession itself, entrenching industry self-policing over outside oversight.
As frequent 'deep pocket' defendants in fraud suits, they benefit from proportionate liability and the new damages formula, which limit what they must pay when a company's fraud is proven.

The bill bans broker referral fees, ties attorneys' fees to amounts actually recovered by the class, restricts sealed settlements, and installs court-appointed overseers of class counsel — cutting the revenue and control of law firms that sue on behalf of defrauded investors.
